facts.statement: Barbaridactylus was first described in 2018 by Nicholas R. Longrich, David M. Martill, and Brian Andres.
facts.quote: It was published in 2018 by paleontologists Nicholas R. Longrich, David M. Martill, and Brian Andres.

facts.statement: Barbaridactylus lived in the Ouled Abdoun Basin of Morocco during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Barbaridactylus is a nyctosaurid pterosaur from the Ouled Abdoun Basin of Morocco, a basin that dates back to the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: All known specimens of Barbaridactylus were found during a three-year excavation that recovered approximately 200 pterosaur fossils.
facts.quote: All known specimens of Barbaridactylus were uncovered in a 3-year dig that unearthed about 200 pterosaur specimens.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Barbaridactylus (FSAC-OB 232) includes a right femur, left radius, ulna, humerus, scapulocoracoid, and a partial mandible.
facts.quote: Its type specimen is FSAC-OB 232, which consists of its right femur, left radius, ulna, humerus, and scapulocoracoid, and partial mandible.

facts.statement: Four additional specimens referred to Barbaridactylus consist entirely of humeri.
facts.quote: Four other specimens have been referred to Barbaridactylus, FSAC-OB 8, 9, 10, and 11. They are all humeri.

facts.statement: The name Barbaridactylus combines a reference to the Barbary Coast of North Africa with the Greek word for "finger".
facts.quote: Barbaridactylus is named after the Barbary Coast of North Africa, and the Greek dactylo, meaning "finger".

facts.statement: Barbaridactylus possessed upward-curving jaws, a trait shared with other nyctosaurids.
facts.quote: Like other nyctosaurids, Barbaridactylus had upward-curving jaws.

facts.statement: The fused scapulocoracoid in Barbaridactylus suggests that the animal was likely an adult.
facts.quote: The scapulocoracoid is fused, meaning that the animal was probably an adult.

facts.statement: Barbaridactylus had a long, thin humeral shaft and a hatchet-shaped deltopectoral crest located distally, resembling that of Nyctosaurus more than Alcione.
facts.quote: The humeral shaft is long and thin. The hatchet-shaped deltopectoral crest (a distinctive feature of nyctosaurids) is in a notably distal location in relation to the humeral head, more similar to that of Nyctosaurus than Alcione.

facts.statement: The ulna of Barbaridactylus is relatively gracile with weakly expanded ends, contrasting with the robust ulna of Alcione.
facts.quote: The ulna is relatively gracile, unlike the robust ulna of Alcione, and its ends are weakly expanded.

facts.statement: The femur of Barbaridactylus expands gently rather than showing the strong distal expansion seen in other nyctosaurids, resembling the femur of Pteranodon.
facts.quote: The femur of Barbaridactylus is relatively typical for a nyctosaurid, although it lacks the strong distal expansion present in other nyctosaurids. Instead, it expands more gently, similar to that of Pteranodon.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis originally placed Barbaridactylus as the sister taxon of Nyctosaurus lamegoi within the family Nyctosauridae.
facts.quote: In this analysis, they found Barbaridactylus to be the sister taxon of the Nyctosaurus species N. lamegoi, both placed within the family Nyctosauridae.

facts.statement: Brian Andres suggested in 2022 that Barbaridactylus might actually be an additional species of Nyctosaurus.
facts.quote: As part of a 2022 monograph on Quetzalcoatlus, Brian Andres suggested that Barbaridactylus may represent an additional species of Nyctosaurus.

facts.statement: A 2024 analysis recovered Barbaridactylus outside the genus Nyctosaurus as the sister taxon of Muzquiopteryx, while reclassifying Nyctosaurus lamegoi as a species of Simurghia.
facts.quote: In a 2024 phylogenetic analysis, Barbaridactylus was recovered as the sister taxon of Muzquiopteryx outside of the genus Nyctosaurus, and "Nyctosaurus" lamegoi was included as a species of Simurghia.

facts.statement: Barbaridactylus fossils were found in upper Maastrichtian phosphates in the Ouled Abdoun Basin of Northern Morocco.
facts.quote: Barbaridactylus was discovered in upper Maastrichtian phosphates located in the Ouled Abdoun Basin of Northern Morocco.

facts.statement: The layer containing Barbaridactylus dates to the latest Maastrichtian, approximately 1 million years before the end-Cretaceous extinction event.
facts.quote: This layer dates back to the latest Maastrichtian, about 1 million years before the extinction event at the end of the Cretaceous.

facts.statement: The ecosystem where Barbaridactylus lived included sharks, bony fish, turtles, plesiosaurs, and mosasaurs.
facts.quote: A large variety of marine life is known from the region, including sharks and bony fish, in addition to turtles, plesiosaurs and mosasaurs.

facts.statement: Recent studies indicate that at least five other pterosaur species, including Alcione, Simurghia, and Tethydraco, lived alongside Barbaridactylus at this location.
facts.quote: However, in addition to Barbaridactylus, more recent studies have revealed at least five more pterosaur species from this location, including Alcione, Simurghia and Tethydraco.

facts.statement: The genus Barbaridactylus was named by Longrich and colleagues in 2018.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Barbaridactylus (genus), Longrich et al. 2018

facts.statement: Barbaridactylus belongs to the family Nyctosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Nyctosauridae

facts.statement: Barbaridactylus is classified as a reptile.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Barbaridactylus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Only one fossil occurrence of Barbaridactylus has been recorded.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 1

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Barbaridactylus is Barbaridactylus grandis.
facts.quote: Type species: Barbaridactylus grandis
